# <span style="font-size: 42px; color: #131516; display: block; margin-bottom: -50px">[**Chapter 15**]{.secondary}: Comparing Mortality Rates</span>

## Standard mortality rates

:::: {.justify .small-text}

[**Standard mortality rates**]{.alert} are mortality rates for a (usually) large reference population. For example, national life tables provide standard mortality rates.

It is often of interest to compare  a set of observed mortality rates, for a study population, with a relevant set of standard rates.

::: {.fragment}

We denote the standard mortality rate at age $x$ by $m^S_x$, and the corresponding observed death count and total exposure in the study population by $D_x$ and $E^C_x$ respectively (it is assumed that the observed and standard rates are comparable in terms of definition).

:::

::: {.fragment}

A [**standardised mortality ratio**]{.alert} $r_x$ at age $x$ is the ratio of the number of observed deaths to the number of deaths expected in the standard population for the same exposure

$$
r_x\;=\;\frac{D_x}{m^S_x E_x^C}\;=\;\frac{\hat{m}_x}{m^S_x}
$$

:::

::::

## Example

:::: {.justify .small-text}

For example, suppose that we observe a regional population of 60-70 year old males over a short period,  and wish to compare observed mortality rates with the interim life tables (England from 2011 to 2013).

| $x$ | $m^S_x$ | $E^C_x$ | $D_x$ | $r_x$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 60 | 0.00794 | 762.0 | 8 | 1.32 |
| 61 | 0.00863 | 755.2 | 10 | 1.53 |
| 62 | 0.00949 | 761.8 | 5 | 0.69 |
| 63 | 0.01019 | 752.0 | 8 | 1.04 |
| 64 | 0.01100 | 733.0 | 13 | 1.61 |
| 65 | 0.01199 | 709.0 | 16 | 1.88 |
| 66 | 0.01330 | 680.8 | 18 | 1.99 |
| 67 | 0.01479 | 657.5 | 12 | 1.23 |
| 68 | 0.01586 | 640.7 | 14 | 1.38 |
| 69 | 0.01781 | 632.0 | 11 | 0.98 |

::: {.fragment}

There seems to be some large discrepancies between mortality rates in our study population and the standard population, i.e. the values of $r_x$ are not close to one.

:::

::::

## Formal comparison by hypothesis test

:::: {.justify}

A formal comparison involves testing the null hypothesis that our observed death pattern has been generated
by the standard rates.

::: {.fragment}

- Rejection of the null hypothesis leads to the conclusion that mortality rates in the study population are significantly different from  the standard rates.
- Non-rejection of the null hypothesis leads to the conclusion that the standard rates could provide a reasonable model for the study population.

:::

::::

## Large sample distributions [**(Gap on page 165)**]{.alert}

:::: {.justify .small-text}

We know that, for the two-state or Poisson models, the central mortality rate

$$
\hat{m}_x\;=\;\frac{D_x}{E^C_x}
$$

is the maximum likelihood estimate for the central mortality rate $m_x$ (equivalently an assumed constant force of mortality $\mu_x$ over $[x,x+1)$), and hence in large samples we can use the normal approximation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat m_x \mathrel{\sim} N\left(m_x,\frac{m_x}{E_x^C}\right) &\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{\hat m_x-m_x}{(m_x/E_x^C)^{1/2}}\mathrel{\sim}N(0,1) \\[2pt]
&\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{(\hat m_x-m_x)^2}{m_x/E_x^C}\mathrel{\sim}\chi_1^2\\[2pt]
&\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{(E_x^C\hat m_x-E_x^C m_x)^2}{E_x^C m_x}\mathrel{\sim}\chi_1^2\\[2pt]
&\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{(D_x-E_x^C m_x)^2}{E_x^C m_x}\mathrel{\sim}\chi_1^2
\end{aligned}
$$

::::

## The chi-squared test

:::: {.justify .small-text}

As we assume that numbers of deaths in different age years are independent, we have that

$$
\sum_x \frac{(D_x-E^C_xm_x)^2}{E^C_xm_x}\;\mathrel{\sim}\;\chi^2_v
$$

where $v$ here is the number of age groups over which mortality rates are being compared.

::: {.fragment}

To test the null hypothesis $H_0$: $m_x=m^S_x$, we have  the test statistic

$$
X^2\;=\;\sum_x \frac{(D_x-E^C_xm^S_x)^2}{E^C_xm^S_x}
$$

and reject $H_0$ if the observed value of $X^2$ is in the upper tail of the $\chi^2_v$ distribution (typically, the threshold for rejection is the $95$-th percentile).

:::

::::

## Return to the example

:::: {.justify .small-text}

For the data in [**Section 15.1**]{.secondary}, we have

$$
X^2\;=\;\frac{(8-6.050)^2}{6.050}+\cdots + \frac{(11-11.256)^2}{11.256}\;=\;23.66
$$

::: {.fragment}

In `R`

```{r}
#| label: mortality-example
#| echo: true
mortality <- data.frame(age = 60:69,
                        mxs = c(0.00794, 0.00863, 0.00949, 0.01019, 0.01100, 0.01199, 0.01330, 0.01479, 0.01586, 0.01781),
                        ECx = c(762.0, 755.2, 761.8, 752.0, 733.0, 709.0, 680.8, 657.5, 640.7, 632.0),
                        dx  = c(8, 10, 5, 8, 13, 16, 18, 12, 14, 11))
head(mortality)

expected <- with(mortality, ECx * mxs)
X2 <- sum((mortality$dx - expected)^2 / expected)
X2
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

We compare this against a chi-squared distribution with $10$ degrees of freedom, and we clearly reject at the 5% level of significance ($\chi^2_{10, 0.95} = 18.31$) and even at the 1% level ($\chi^2_{10, 0.99} = 23.21$).

:::

::::

## Return to the example {.limit-code-3}

:::: {.justify .small-text}

In `R`, the quantiles of the $\chi^2$ are

```{r}
#| echo: true
print(paste(round(qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 10), 2), round(qchisq(p = 0.99, df = 10), 2)))
```

Also,

```{r, echo = TRUE, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 2.5, fig.align = "center"}
df <- 10
critical <- qchisq(0.95, df)
x <- seq(0, 30, length.out = 1000)
tail <- seq(critical, 30, length.out = 500)

plot(x, dchisq(x, df), type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "",
     xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", yaxt = "n", bty = "n")
polygon(c(critical, tail, 30), c(0, dchisq(tail, df), 0),
        density = 8, angle = 45, border = NA)
lines(x, dchisq(x, df))
```

::: {style="margin-top: -60pt;"}
$\chi^2_{10}$ distribution with upper $5\%$ tail indicated.
:::

::: {.fragment}

We can also calculate a p-value in `R`

```{r}
#| label: chi-squared-p-value
#| echo: true
pchisq(q = X2, df = 10, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

:::

::::


## Chi-squared test properties

:::: {.justify .small-text}

A general rule of thumb is that conclusions from a chi-squared test can be considered reliable if all of the
$E^C_xm^S_x$ values are greater than $1$, and no more than $20\%$ of them are less than $5$.

The chi-squared test is usually a very sound [**omnibus**]{.alert} test; i.e., [it can detect a wide range of discrepancies between a set of observed and standard rates.]{.secondary}

::: {.fragment}

However, other tests exist which can be more powerful to detect particular kinds of discrepancy, in particular,

- [**Bias**]{.secondary}, where the observed rates are generally higher or lower than the standard rates.

- [**Patterns of differences**]{.secondary}, where there are parts of the age spectrum with positive bias (observed rates higher than standard) and parts of the age spectrum with negative bias.

- [**Extreme differences**]{.secondary}, where there are a small number of age groups where the observed and standard rates are very different.

:::

::::

## Multiple comparisons

:::: {.justify .small-text}

Caution is required when performing multiple tests of (essentially) the same hypothesis (goodness-of-fit of standard mortality rates to a set of observed rates).

If we have a hypothesis which is true, and we perform $5$ independent tests of the hypothesis then, with probability $1-0.95^5=0.226$, we will observe at least one significant result (at the $5\%$ level).

So, sound advice is to just use a single test, usually an omnibus chi-squared test unless you have an a priori reason to expect a particular kind of discrepancy.

::: {.fragment}

- [**If the null hypothesis is rejected**]{.secondary}, examine the patterns of observed and standard rates to identify why there is a significant difference.

- [**If the null hypothesis is not rejected**]{.secondary}, you can still examine the patterns of observed and standard rates to investigate whether there might be any cause for concern about a discrepancy not detected by your omnibus test, but be cautious about any further formal hypothesis testing.

:::

::::

## Other tests

:::: {.justify .small-text}

Bearing in mind the caution advised in using further tests, we will introduce some other possible tests to detect differences between observed and standard mortality rates.

::: {.fragment}

- Bias
  - Cumulative deviations test
  - Sign test
- Patterns of differences
  - Difference of signs test
  - Serial correlation test
  - Grouping of signs test (not recommended) – better to use the Wald–Wolfowitz runs test
- Extreme differences
  - Examination of individual standardised differences


We consider tests for bias.

:::

::::

## Tests for bias: Cumulative deviations test

:::: {.justify .small-text}

We recall from [**Section 15.3**]{.secondary} that we have the approximation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat m_x &\mathrel{\sim} N\left(m_x,\frac{m_x}{E_x^C}\right)\\[2pt]
&\Rightarrow\quad
\sum_x E_x^C\hat m_x\mathrel{\sim}
N\left(\sum_x E_x^C m_x,\sum_x E_x^C m_x\right)\\[2pt]
&\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{\sum_x (D_x-E_x^C m_x)}{\left(\sum_x E_x^C m_x\right)^{1/2}}
\mathrel{\sim} N(0,1)
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment}

To test the null hypothesis $H_0$: $m_x=m^S_x$, we have  the test statistic

$$
Z\;=\;\frac{\sum_x (D_x-E^C_xm^S_x)}{\left(\sum_xE^C_xm^S_x\right)^{1/2}}
$$

and reject $H_0$ if $z$,  the observed value of $Z$, is in either tail of the standard normal distribution (typically, the threshold for rejection is $|z|>1.96$, giving a significance level of $5\%$).

:::

::::

## Tests for bias: Sign test

:::: {.justify .small-text}

The sign test is easy to apply, but generally has low power.
The test statistic for the sign test is $S=\sum_x U_x$ where

$$
U_x\;=\;\left\{
\begin{array}{lll}
1&\mbox{if }\hat{m}_x\ge m^S_x&\quad\mbox{(so $\hat{m}_x- m^S_x$ has a non-negative sign)}\\
0&\mbox{if }\hat{m}_x<m^S_x&\quad\mbox{(so $\hat{m}_x- m^S_x$ has a negative sign)}\\
\end{array}\right.
$$

::: {.fragment}

Under the null hypothesis $H_0$: $m_x=m^S_x$, we have that the $U_x$ are independent and use the approximation $\mathbb{P}(U_x=1)\approx 0.5$, and therefore that the reference distribution of $S$ is binomial$(v,0.5)$ where $v$ is the number of age groups.

:::

::: {.fragment}

We reject $H_0$ if the observed value of $S$ is in either tail of the binomial.

For all but very small values of $v$, a normal approximation to the binomial can be used, so we reject  $H_0$ if $|z|>z_{1-\alpha/2}$, at significance level $\alpha$, where $z$ is the observed value of

$$
Z\;=\;\frac{S\pm\frac{1}{2}-\frac{v}{2}}{\left(\frac{v}{4}\right)^{1/2}}.
$$

Note the continuity correction ($+\frac{1}{2}$ if $S<\frac{v}{2}$, $-\frac{1}{2}$ if $S>\frac{v}{2}$).

:::

::::

## Return to the example: Cumulative deviations test

:::: {.justify .small-text}

For the data in [**Section 15.1**]{.secondary}, we have, for the cumulative deviations test, $\sum_x D_x=115$ and $\sum_x E^C_xm^S_x=84.220$, and therefore

$$
z\;=\;\frac{115-84.220}{84.220^{1/2}}\;=\;3.354
$$

The $0.975$-th quantile of $N(0,1)$ is $z_{0.975} = 1.96$. So $\mathrm{H}_0$ is rejected at $5\%$ level.

::::

## Return to the example: Cumulative deviations test in `R`

:::: {.justify .small-text}

In `R`

```{r}
#| label: cumulative-deviations
#| echo: true
Z <- sum(mortality$dx - expected) / sqrt(sum(expected))
Z
qnorm(0.975)
```

::: {.fragment}

Can also calculate a p-value

```{r}
#| label: cumulative-deviations-p-value
#| echo: true
2 * pnorm(abs(Z), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

:::

::::

## Return to the example: Sign test 

:::: {.justify .small-text}

For the sign test, $u=(1,1,0,1,1,1,1,1,1,0)$ and  therefore $s=8$ and

$$
z\;=\;\frac{7.5-5}{2.5^{1/2}}\;=\;1.581
$$

This is not significant at the $5\%$ level of significance since $z_{0.975} = 1.96$.

::::

## Return to the example: Sign test in `R`

:::: {.justify .small-text}

In `R`

```{r}
#| label: sign-test-normal
#| echo: true
v <- nrow(mortality)
S <- sum(mortality$dx >= expected)
correction <- 0.5 * sign(v / 2 - S)
Z_sign <- (S + correction - v / 2) / sqrt(v / 4)
S
Z_sign
2 * pnorm(abs(Z_sign), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.fragment}

The actual binomial p-value (probability of observing $S=8$ or more extreme) is $0.109$ (very similar).

```{r}
#| label: sign-test-exact
#| echo: true
binom.test(S, v, p = 0.5)$p.value
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

This illustrates the lack of power of the sign test.

:::

::::
